title: Abstract nouns
keyIdea: A noun names something. A concrete noun names something you can see, hear, touch, taste or smell: a table, a puppy. An abstract noun names something you cannot: a feeling (joy, fear), a quality a person has (honesty, courage) or an idea, time or state (freedom, childhood, peace). Many abstract nouns are built from a describing word plus an ending: kind + ness = kindness, enjoy + ment = enjoyment, child + hood = childhood, friend + ship = friendship, free + dom = freedom. Use the noun after words like her, your or his (her bravery) and the describing word after felt or were (we felt proud).
familyTip: Play the touch test at dinner. Say a noun, and your child taps the table if you could touch it, or taps their head if it lives only in your head: spoon, kindness, bread, fear, holiday, patience. Then swap: they say kind, you say kindness. Who can turn the most describing words into nouns?

visual.caption: Is each noun concrete or abstract? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort nouns by the touch test, build nouns with -ness, -ment, -hood, -ship and -dom, fill noun or describing word gaps, and spot abstract nouns.

kid: A noun is a naming word. Some nouns name things you can see or touch, like a dog or a cup. These are concrete nouns.
Some nouns name things you cannot touch: joy, fear, kindness, freedom. You feel them or think them. These are abstract nouns. They are still nouns.
You can make an abstract noun by adding an ending. kind becomes kindness. child becomes childhood. friend becomes friendship. happy becomes happiness: the y turns to i.
Her bravery helped the team. bravery is the noun. She was brave. brave is the describing word.
adult: Ages 8 to 9. Common Core L.3.1c asks children to explain the function of nouns and to use abstract nouns (its own example is childhood). In England, the Year 2 grammar appendix teaches forming nouns with suffixes such as -ness, and Years 3 and 4 build word families. A concrete noun names something perceived by the senses; an abstract noun names a feeling, a quality, an idea or a state that cannot be.

The suffixes in the lab each make abstract nouns: -ness (kindness, happiness), -ment (enjoyment), -hood (childhood), -ship (friendship) and -dom (freedom). Spelling rules still apply: y after a consonant turns to i (happiness). Many abstract nouns are not built from a suffix at all (joy, fear, peace), so the touch test is the check that always works.

Common mistakes: thinking a noun must be a thing you can hold, so joy or courage cannot be a noun; using the describing word where a noun is needed (her brave helped the team) or the noun where a describing word is needed (we felt pride); adding the wrong ending (kindment, childness); and spelling slips such as happyness.

In the lab your child sorts eight nouns by the touch test, builds six abstract nouns by dragging an ending onto a word, chooses between the noun and the describing word for five gaps, taps the abstract noun in five sentences that also contain concrete nouns, and groups nine abstract nouns into feelings, qualities, and times or states.

practice.prompt: Which word is an abstract noun?
practice.hint: Which one can you not see or touch?
practice.explain: You can see a pencil and touch a river, so they are concrete. Courage is a quality you cannot touch, so it is an abstract noun.

practice.prompt: A list has {n} nouns. {k} of them name things you can touch. How many are abstract nouns?
practice.hint: Every noun is either concrete or abstract. Take the concrete ones away.
practice.explain: {n} nouns take away {k} concrete ones leaves {=n-k} abstract nouns.

practice.hint: After your, the sentence needs a naming word.
practice.explain: After your we need a noun: kindness. kind describes a person, and kindly tells how something is done.

practice.prompt: Mia adds -ness to {a} describing words and -ship to {b} nouns. How many new abstract nouns does she make?
practice.hint: Each word plus its ending makes one new noun. Add them up.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} new abstract nouns, such as kindness and friendship.

practice.hint: happy ends in a consonant then y. What happens to the y before -ness?
practice.explain: Change y to i, then add -ness: happiness. happyness keeps the y, and happyment uses the wrong ending.

pool.prompt: In 'The children shouted with joy', which word is the abstract noun?
pool.hint: Find the noun you cannot see or touch.
pool.explain: You can see children, so it is a concrete noun. shouted is a verb. joy is a feeling, so it is the abstract noun.

pool.prompt: child + ___ = the time when you are a child
pool.explain: child + hood = childhood. childness and childment are not words.

pool.prompt: We felt ___ when we won the match.
pool.hint: After felt, use a describing word.
pool.explain: After felt we need a describing word: proud. pride is the noun, as in 'our pride'.

pool.prompt: Which group is all abstract nouns?
pool.hint: Check every word with the touch test.
pool.explain: fear, honesty and freedom cannot be touched. honey and chair can, so those groups have a concrete noun.

choices: It names something, even though you cannot touch it.
pool.hint: A noun names something. Can you put the in front of it?
pool.explain: friendship names a relationship, and you can say the friendship or our friendship, so it is a noun. It is abstract because you cannot touch it.

pool.prompt: A poem has {n} nouns. {k} are concrete. How many are abstract?
pool.hint: Take the concrete nouns away from all the nouns.
Say enjoy with each ending. Which one is a real word?
pool.explain: enjoy + ment = enjoyment. enjoyness and enjoydom are not words.

pool.prompt: Sam writes {a} sentences with an abstract noun each day for {d} days. How many sentences does he write?
pool.explain: {a} × {d} = {=a*d} sentences, using words like kindness and freedom.

pool.hint: After her, the sentence needs a noun.
pool.explain: After her we need a noun: bravery. brave describes, and bravely says how something is done.
